name: ctbignum
workload: Fixed-width multiplication of 2, 4 and 8 64-bit-limb integers (100-500 bit range), run time and compile time.
claimed_speedup: 2 limbs: 4 ns vs GMP 14 ns (3.5x); 4 limbs: 18 ns vs 29 ns (1.6x); 8 limbs: 85 ns vs GMP 67 ns (GMP 1.3x faster)
hardware: 2017 MacBook Pro, quad-core 2.3 GHz Intel Core i5 (Kaby Lake), 16 GB, Turbo Boost disabled
tradeoffs: Fixed-width only (sizes known at compile time), C++20 header-only; wins only for small limb counts via inlining and unrolling.
caveats: GMP is faster at 8 limbs; numbers from the 2018 paper on 2017 hardware; benchmark code is in the repo (needs GMP, NTL, libff, Google Benchmark) but I did not open the benchmark directory itself.
found_via: WebSearch: intx uint256 C++ fixed width big integer faster than GMP benchmark -> arXiv 1804.07236

name: mp++
workload: 1-limb unsigned integer dot product, vector multiply-add and vector division over small operands (also compared with Boost.Multiprecision cpp_int/gmp_int and FLINT fmpzxx).
claimed_speedup: dot product: almost 4 times faster than GMP; multiply-add: more than 7 times faster; division: about 8 times faster (mp++ and FLINT)
tradeoffs: C++ wrapper built on GMP/MPFR/MPC; small-value optimisation (inline limbs) beats GMP only for small operands.
caveats: Docs state no compiler, flags or CPU. Advantage is limited to 1-limb values; large operands defer to GMP.
found_via: WebSearch: C++ big integer arbitrary precision library faster than GMP benchmark github

name: FLINT
baseline: GMP (mpz_t, pi via Chudnovsky) and MPFR (mpfr_const_pi)
workload: 100 million digits of pi (arb_const_pi) and 100x100 integer matrix multiplication with fmpz_t versus mpz_t.
claimed_speedup: pi to 100M digits: GMP 62.1 s, MPFR 172.9 s, FLINT 31.6 s (about 2x GMP, 5x MPFR); 8 threads 9.34 s; fmpz_t about 3x faster than mpz_t with small entries (b=10: 0.0122 s GMP vs 0.0000678 s FLINT optimized)
tradeoffs: Built on top of GMP/MPFR; matrix claim compares FLINT's optimized algorithms with naive GMP loops.
caveats: First-party page; no compiler or flags and no benchmark code link on the page; the matrix comparison is algorithmic (multimodular), not a like-for-like mpz kernel; dual LGPL/GPL.
found_via: WebSearch: FLINT fmpz arb arbitrary-precision ball arithmetic faster than MPFR benchmark

name: Arb
workload: Arbitrary-precision dot product and matrix multiplication at 53-212+ bit precision (Table I, cycles per term).
claimed_speedup: about twice as fast as MPFR at several hundred bits, 3-4 times up to 128 bits; Table I: 212 bits 133 vs 208 cycles/term, 106 bits 49 vs 156, 53 bits 40 vs 99
tradeoffs: Ball (midpoint-radius interval) arithmetic, so not a drop-in MPFR replacement; carries error bounds.
caveats: Repo is archived because Arb was merged into FLINT; use FLINT for current code. Compiler flags unstated in the paper; measured with GMP 6.1 and MPFR 4.0 in Dec 2018. Repo README also gives a hypergeometric table vs MPFR, which I did not use. Same code now lives in FLINT, so consider folding into the FLINT entry.
found_via: WebSearch: FLINT fmpz arb arbitrary-precision ball arithmetic faster than MPFR benchmark

name: Boost.Multiprecision (cpp_int fixed-precision)
workload: Fixed-width (128 and 256-bit) cpp_int arithmetic operators (+, -, *, &, ^, construct) versus gmp_int, relative-time tables.
claimed_speedup: 128-bit operator*: cpp_int(fixed) 1.0 (best) vs gmp_int 4.80 relative time; 128-bit operator+(int): 1.0 vs 4.98; fixed cpp_int best for 128-256 bit +,-,^,* (relative-time tables)
tradeoffs: Header-only; fixed-precision types avoid heap allocation, dynamic cpp_int loses to GMP at 512+ bits.
caveats: Docs from Sept 2021 (GMP 6.2.0, Boost 1.78), CPU not stated, flags not stated; GMP wins at larger sizes and by ~11x on Miller-Rabin modular exponentiation (derived from page data: 0.0497s vs 0.00443s). Win limited to small fixed widths.
found_via: WebSearch: Boost.Multiprecision cpp_int faster than GMP benchmark fixed precision small integers
